Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:3: And it says afterward, of blessed memory: upon the brain rests blessing, upon the heart rests holiness, upon the lung rests unity; thought comprises them all — and these are "May the Lord bless you," "may the Lord shine [His face]," "may the Lord lift up [His face]" — "may He bless you" in the brain; "may He shine" in the heart, where is the light of the eyes; "may He lift up" in the lung, which is peace — this is what is written, "and give you peace" — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:4: This passage makes clear that holiness resides in the heart. The reason for this is explained by Rashbi, peace be upon him (Zohar Parashat Shelach 161a), that a person is a model of a small world, and there is in a person an allusion to the world, to the Temple and the Holy of Holies; and it says that the heart corresponds to the Holy of Holies, in these words: Come and see, when the Holy One, blessed be He, created man in the world, He arranged him in the precious supernal manner, and gave him his strength and vigor in the middle of the body, where the heart rests, which is the strength and sustenance of the whole body, and from there the whole body is nourished, and all the limbs of the body are nourished from there; and the heart takes hold and grasps the supernal place above, which is the brain of the head, resting above, and takes hold of it, and this is bound to that. In this manner the Holy One, blessed be He, arranged and made him one body, and arranged the limbs of the body around the heart, and the heart rests in the middle, and the whole body and all those limbs are nourished from that heart, which is the strength of all, and everything depends on it, and that heart is bound and grasped to the supernal brain that rests above. So it is: when the Holy One, blessed be He, created the world, He arranged the Ocean Sea, which surrounds all the inhabited world; and the settlement of all seventy nations surrounds Jerusalem, and Jerusalem rests in the middle of all the settlement, and it surrounds the Temple Mount, and the Temple Mount surrounds the courtyards of Israel, and those courtyards surround the Chamber of Hewn Stone, where the Great Sanhedrin sits — and we have learned, there is no sitting in the courtyard except for the kings of the House of David alone — and the Chamber of Hewn Stone surrounds the House of the Portico, and the Portico [surrounds] the altar, and the altar surrounds the Sanctuary, and the Sanctuary [surrounds] the House of the Holy of Holies, where the Shechinah rests, and the covering (kaporet) and the cherubim and the Ark; and here is the heart of the whole earth and the world, and from here all those places of settlement are nourished, which are the limbs of the body; and the heart is nourished from the brain of the head, and this is bound with that — this is what is written, "the place, O Lord, which You have made for Your dwelling" (Exodus 15:17) — in this manner, above and higher still, and so on — so far his words, as pertains to us. And further on it explains, in the passage, that all these aspects, both in this world and in the Temple, exist likewise above, and higher still above — but this does not pertain to our discourse.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:5: It follows from this, for our intent, that the heart in a person corresponds to the House of the Holy of Holies, in which are the Ark and the covering and the cherubim; and we learn from this that just as the Shechinah rested in the Temple because there was there the Ark, the Tablets, the cherubim, and so on, so too a person's heart should be prepared so that the Shechinah rests within it, and it becomes a Holy of Holies. And so it is explained in the Tikkunim (140b), that concerning the wings of the lung it is said, "and the cherubim shall spread their wings on high, covering the covering (kaporet) with their wings" (Exodus 25:20), and they said, of blessed memory: "the kaporet" — this is the atonement (kapparah) of the heart; "the Holy of Holies" — this is the heart — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:6: And there (13b) it explains another aspect of the heart, saying that the Ark that was in the Tabernacle corresponded to the heart, in these words: the Ark, certainly, is the heart, and the lit lamp comprises the thirty-two paths, and this is Shabbat, and in it is the supernal Shechinah, which is "the Torah of the wise," and through her the heart understands. And further on it says: the covering (kaporet) of the heart is the separation of the "tabernacle of peace," of which it is said, "He who spreads the tabernacle of peace" — so far his words. The intent is that the Ark corresponds to the heart, which is the Shechinah comprised of thirty-two paths — for the heart is the Shechinah, as is explained in the Tikkunim (49b), which says, "the heart understands, the heart knows, the heart sees — she is the Shechinah," and so on. And so in the Tikkunim in manuscript (Tikkunei Zohar Chadash 114b), regarding "let us make man," nine limbs are counted, and it says there, "let us make man" — behold, the heart, which is the completion of all; the intent being that it is the tenth aspect, corresponding to the Shechinah, as expounded there with regard to the other limbs. And it says, "the heart understands" — the intent being that the supernal Shechinah bestows within it the power of understanding, so that the heart understands.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:7: And in Tikkun 25 (Tikkunim 70a) it says that the five wings of the lung, with the "rose" (varda), which together are six, correspond to the Seraphim, of whom it is said, "each had six wings, six wings each" (Isaiah 6:2); and it says that these six are from the side of the letter Vav, which is the Torah scroll — the Ark of the Torah scroll being the throne of the heart, which is a burning fire; and were it not for the wings of the lung fanning it, the heart would burn up the whole body — that fire being the blood in the arteries of the heart, and the spirit (ruach) blows in the arteries of blood, and all are conducted after it, this being what is written, "wherever the spirit was to go, they went" (Ezekiel 1:12) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:8: This spirit that cools the blood of judgment is from the side of Tiferet, who is the Master of Mercy; and so it explains further on: when the spirit comes to the heart, where the nefesh is, of it is said, "the voice of my beloved knocking" (Song of Songs 5:2).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:9: And so it is further explained in the Tikkunim (53a), in these words: this ruach, wherever it is found, is the supernal and lower Shechinah; it is the Vav that blows in the wings of the lung, and upon the heart, where is the lamp of the Lord — this is the neshamah in the brain, the ruach in the wings of the lung, the nefesh in the heart. And sometimes three [correspond] to three brains, and Thought rides upon them, which is Adam. And so, three [correspond] to the heart — Nun-Reish, neshamah, ruach, which blow into two chambers of the heart, being nefesh and ruach, the sign N-R (ner, lamp). And this Vav is what blows in the arms, in their six joints, and it blows in the two legs, which are "his legs are pillars of marble" (Song of Songs 5:15); and concerning this it is said, "and the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him" (Isaiah 11:2) — when the limbs of the body are conducted with this spirit through the commandments of the Torah, the ship is conducted in every direction a person wishes, as it is said, "wherever the spirit was to go, they went" — the ship being the head, the heart, and the body. And if the ten limbs of the body, which are the masters of the ship, being the holy people, are not conducted by the Torah, which is the neshamah, [and] by the mitzvah, which is the nefesh, the spirit flies from among them, and at that time, "and the Lord cast a great wind (ruach) upon the sea" (Jonah 1:4), which is a stormy wind — a harsh decree of judgment that disturbs the very body of the person, who are Israel, and Israel are in the storm, and the ship, which is the body, threatens to break up — so far his words, as pertains to us.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:10: At the beginning of the passage it explains that neshamah, ruach, nefesh have their dwellings — neshamah in the brain, ruach in the wings of the lung, nefesh in the heart. And so it is also explained in the Tikkunim (49a), in these words: further, the neshamah, ruach, and nefesh of a person are teruah, tekiah, shevarim — the nefesh in the heart, and this is shevarim (broken sounds), as it is said, "a broken and crushed heart" (Psalms 51:19); the neshamah in the brain, and this is tekiah (a straight blast); the ruach in the wings of the lung that blow upon the heart, and this is teruah (a tremulous blast), and so on — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:11: What pertains to practice from this matter is made clear in the passage: that when one is occupied with Torah and commandments, this ruach spreads throughout the whole body, for this ruach is the inner aspect of Da'at (knowledge), the neshamah spreading within the six extremities; this is [the meaning of] "wherever the spirit was to go, they went." And if not, God forbid, this holy ruach withdraws, and a stormy wind rules, which is harsh judgment, and then "the ship threatened to break up."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:12: Further, it says in the Tikkunim (end of 140b), in these words: nefesh, ruach, and neshamah [correspond to] Kohen, Levi, and Yisrael. Kohen is the neshamah — if he merits it, [it becomes] "the lamp of the Lord"; the lamp shines within him from the heart like the radiant sun, and the holy spirit goes forth from between the wings of the cherubim, which are the wings of the lung, and it speaks with him. But if not, fire — this is the nefesh — fire goes forth from the heart and burns him — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:13: Similar to this, they further explain there, just before this, in these words: the kidneys are the ones that counsel — if they merit it, prophecy enters them, which is "the lamp of the Lord, the soul of man," and they become prophets and counsel for good, and there is counsel and sound wisdom in them. The wings of the lung — if they merit it, a holy spirit rests within them, and it is said of them, "and the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and fear of the Lord" (Isaiah 11:2), and concerning them it is said, "and the cherubim shall spread out their wings..." (Exodus 25:20, adapted) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:14: What pertains to the holiness of the heart is two aspects: one positive, one negative. The positive aspect is this: since the nefesh's place is in the heart, as is made clear in the passages we quoted, the holiness of the nefesh is the holiness of performing the commandments, as we explained above in chapter 4, quoting the wording of Rashbi (Tikkunei Zohar 68b), who said, "'I made it' — this is the nefesh, in which there is deed, resting within the two hundred forty-eight commandments." This matter is what the verse is precise about in saying, "and you shall not go astray after your heart... that you may remember and do all My commandments and be holy..." (Numbers 15:39-40) — it appears that the rectification of the heart is through performing the commandments, and by this it becomes sanctified.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:15: We further learn from the words of Rashbi, who said that the "pocket" of the heart is the Ark; and it is known (Bava Batra 14b) that within the Ark were the Tablets and the broken pieces of the Tablets. So too one's heart should be filled with Torah, and the spirit blowing from the wings of the lung, which is Vav, should blow within it the light of the air of Torah as is fitting, and one will merit the holy spirit, at the level of the High Priest, as is explained in the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:16: Corresponding to the broken pieces of the Tablets, one's heart must be a "broken and crushed heart," so that it be a foundation for the Shechinah — for the Shechinah's dwelling is among her "broken vessels," as is explained in Parashat Vayikra (Zohar 9a), and these are the poor whose hearts are broken and crushed. And whoever's heart is haughty pushes the Shechinah away from him, as it is said, "an abomination to the Lord is every haughty heart" (Proverbs 16:5); and so Rashbi, peace be upon him, explains it in the Tikkunim (69b), in these words: and the haughtiness of a heart that is whole with its own kelipot and not broken, of it is said, "an abomination to the Lord is every haughty heart," and the Shechinah does not rest upon it — so far his words. And in the Gate of Awe, chapter 4, we quoted his full wording.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:17: There is no doubt that even the nefesh residing in the heart withdraws, since he has brought into the heart a kelipah that pushes her away — for holiness does not rest in a place where there is an outsider — "evil shall not sojourn with You" (Psalms 5:5) — and the proof is that when they brought an idol into the Sanctuary, the Shechinah withdrew. So too every blemish a person causes in his heart, from envy, hatred, anger, and rivalry, is as though bringing an idol into the Sanctuary of the Holy of Holies, since it has already been explained that the heart is the Holy of Holies. This is the negative aspect — that one must be careful of all these, so that his heart be a holy vessel in which the Shechinah rests, and the Shechinah should not find, God forbid, any blemish of an outsider that would push her away.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:18: Just as we were warned on the day of Shabbat against anger and sadness, as Rashbi, peace be upon him, says in the Tikkunim (Tikkun 24, 69b), so one must be careful on the six weekdays as well. This is the wording of Rashbi, peace be upon him, in Tikkun 48 (85a): fortunate is he who guards his dwelling for Shabbat — that is, his heart, into which the sadness of the spleen and the anger of the gall bladder, which is the fire of Gehinnom, does not draw near — concerning which it is said, "you shall kindle no fire throughout your dwellings on the Sabbath day" (Exodus 35:3); and it is certainly so that whoever grows angry is as though he kindled the fire of Gehinnom — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:19: Certainly this warning is one we always need — not to grow angry even on weekdays, so as not to kindle the fire of Gehinnom — but on the day of Shabbat the blemish is without end, for since the fire of Gehinnom is entirely nullified [on that day], and this person kindles it anew, his punishment is very great. On the day of Shabbat a person must be slow to anger and utterly humble, and he should learn from the attributes of his Maker: on the day of Shabbat He is patient toward the wicked in Gehinnom, for the fire of Gehinnom is nullified, as is explained in Parashat Yitro (89a): because of the revealing of the Ancient One, all anger and all judgments are stilled on the day of Shabbat. And how many idolaters are before Him, and He is patient! And through the trait of humility that one acquires on the day of Shabbat, one should draw it into all six days, for the day of Shabbat is the root of all holinesses, as we explained in chapter 2, and shall further explain, please God.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:20: And so, just as one must guard himself from sadness of heart, so must he on the weekdays, for the Shechinah does not rest from a state of sadness, and so on, but from a state of joy, as is explained in the Gemara (Shabbat 30b) — except at times that require sadness, such as during the four fasts on which one fasts for the destruction of the Temple, when there is sadness even before Him, as is explained in the Gemara (Chagigah 13a), that in the inner chambers there is sadness. And so they said in tractate Berachot, chapter 1 (3a), "the night has three watches, and at every single watch the Holy One, blessed be He...," as explained there — at these times sadness is good. Or if one is saddened over his sins, none of this is a blemish to the heart; but the sadness that is on account of matters of this world is what causes the blemish.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:21: One must be the same inside as outside; its mystery is explained in the Tikkunim (128b), in these words: whoever is from the Tree of Life is the same inside as outside, mouth and heart being equal, and concerning them it is said, "and take also from the Tree of Life, and eat, and live forever" (Genesis 3:22). But another, whose mouth and heart are not equal, of him it is said, "but of the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil you shall not eat of it" — for he is certainly an evil mixture that counterfeits the King's coinage, mixing silver with lead, and so on — so far his words, as pertains to us; and its mystery will be further explained regarding prayer, please God. One must speak truth in his heart, for by this one causes the unification of the attribute of Truth in the heart, and this is the mystery of "Truth shall spring up from the earth" (Psalms 85:12).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:22: The general principle is: since the heart is the source of life, situated in the middle of the body, and it corresponds to the House of the Holy of Holies, which is the middle point for the world, all the good qualities of the limbs flow from the heart, and likewise in reverse. Therefore they said in tractate Avot (2:9), in the Mishnah of the five disciples of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai: Rabbi Eliezer says, a good eye, and so on; Rabbi Elazar says, a good heart; and he [Rabban Yochanan] said, I see the words of Elazar ben Arach as greater than yours, for his words include your words. And likewise in reverse, an evil heart is the root of all disgraceful qualities.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:23: Further, they said in the Gemara Nedarim (20b) and Yalkut (remez 750), in explanation of the verse, "and you shall not go astray after your heart" (Numbers 15:39): from here Rabbi Natan said, a person should not drink from this cup and set his eye on another cup. Rava said, this is needed only [to teach] even regarding his two wives. Another interpretation: "and you shall not go astray after your heart and after your eyes" — this teaches that the eyes follow the heart. Or perhaps the heart follows the eyes? You may say, but is there not a blind man who commits all the abominations of the world? So what does the verse teach by "and you shall not go astray after your heart"? This teaches that the eyes follow the heart. And it further says there: Rabbi Yitzchak said, the heart and the eye are two brokers of sin — "and you shall not go astray," and so on; "Give me your heart, my son, and let your eyes observe my ways" (Proverbs 23:26); the Holy One, blessed be He, said, if you have given Me your heart and your eye, I know that you are Mine — so far his words. This makes clear that the heart is the source of all qualities, whether for good or the reverse; therefore the verse mentions the heart before the eyes: "you shall not go astray after your heart," and afterward "after your eyes"; and so, "Give me your heart, my son, and your eyes..."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:24: According to our Rabbis, of blessed memory, who said, "if you have given Me your heart and your eye," one must say that the plain sense of the verse is, "Give me your heart, my son" — and here the verse pauses briefly — "and your eyes shall observe my ways." And the reason the verse does not say, "Give me your heart and your eyes," together, is because the heart is the essential thing, as is explained in the passage that says, "the eyes follow the heart."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:25: Thus far we have discussed what pertains to the particulars of the heart. But regarding what pertains to the general holiness of thoughts, dependent on the two [organs] mentioned, the brain and the heart, there are further particulars alluded to in the verses and in the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, and these are the essential matter for the holiness of thought.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:26: The first of these is that one should constantly rise every night at midnight and occupy himself with Torah until daybreak. Among the special properties of rising at midnight to occupy oneself with Torah are great virtues that will be explained, please God, one of them being the subduing of the kelipot. This matter is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Vayechi 242a), on the verse, "Issachar is a large-boned donkey" (Genesis 49:14); it opens and says, "The Lord is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear; the Lord is the strength of my life, of whom shall I be afraid" (Psalms 27:1). How beloved are the words of Torah! How beloved are those who occupy themselves with Torah before the Holy One, blessed be He! For whoever occupies himself with Torah does not fear the mishaps of the world; he is guarded above, he is guarded below, and not only that, but he subdues all the mishaps of the world and casts them down into the depths of the great abyss.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:27: Come and see, at the hour night enters, the gates are shut, and dogs and donkeys are set loose and roam the world, and license is given to harm, and all the people of the world sleep in their beds, and the souls of the righteous ascend to delight above. When the north wind stirs and the night is divided, a holy arousal is aroused in the world, and it is said in several places: fortunate is the portion of that person who stands at that hour and occupies himself with Torah. Once he opens with Torah, all those evil kinds are brought down into the caverns of the great abyss, and the donkey is subdued and brought down into the muddy depths beneath the dust of the vile encampment. Therefore Issachar, whose occupation is Torah, subdues the donkey and brings it down from that ascent of stairs which rises to harm the world, and places its dwelling among the sheepfolds, among the muddy depths of dust — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:28: We have already elaborated above that the confusion of thoughts that comes upon a person at the time of standing in prayer or occupying himself with Torah is because of his sins, which make him unfit to unify [the sefirot], and the sin is the external accuser that interposes between him and his God. Since this person is accustomed to rise at midnight to occupy himself with Torah, he subdues the Other Side, and his sins are atoned for; and by this he comes to purify his thought, and his unification is not confused.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:29: The reason for this may be said to be that the attribute of night is what flows forth the judgments, and from it the external judgments nurse; and it is transformed from darkness to light — meaning, from the attribute of Judgment to the attribute of Mercy — through occupation with Torah, and since it is sweetened, all those [forces] dependent on it are likewise sweetened. Further, the harshest of all kelipot is death, and sleep is one-sixtieth of death (Berachot 57b); and when a person drives sleep from his eyes, the harshest kelipah is found broken, and certainly all the rest will of themselves be subdued and broken, and the light of the pupil of the eye will shine through the light of Torah. Therefore King David, peace be upon him, did not sleep at night more than sixty "breaths" (Sukkah 26b, Zohar Parashat Vayigash 207a), for the reason stated; and so every penitent must drive sleep from his eyes at night through occupation with Torah and prayer, in order to subdue the kelipot, and he will certainly have great assistance for his repentance.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:30: And so it says in the Tikkunim (Tikkun 50, 86b): and all this is sustained according to people's deeds. Fortunate is he who raises her [the Shechinah] to her place, and the Holy One, blessed be He, to His place, concerning whom it is said, "Behold, the Lord rides upon a swift cloud" (Isaiah 19:1), "Behold, the Lord goes forth from His place" (Isaiah 26:21). Rabbi Elazar said to him, Father, can a person really return the Holy One, blessed be He, to His place? Yes — as I found regarding David, who said, "I will not give sleep to my eyes, nor slumber to my eyelids, until I find a place for the Lord..." (Psalms 132:4-5). At that time, when a person returns Him to His place, what is written of it? "From His place He shall turn in mercy to His people..." and so on — so far his words. This makes it explicit that King David, peace be upon him, by driving sleep from his eyes, returned the Holy One, blessed be He, to His place; and every single individual should learn from him — since through his sin he causes the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah to be exiled from their place, as is explained in the Gate of Awe, it is fitting that he return in repentance and drive sleep from his eyes to return them to their place.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:31: And so, when a person considers that after his death his eyes will be shut from seeing, how much he will then regret his past and say, "While my eyes were still open, why did I not use them to occupy myself with Torah, and drive sleep from my eyes?" Therefore, while there is still breath of life within him, he should distance himself from death and attach himself to Torah, which is the Tree of Life — in the manner explained in the Zohar, Parashat Naso (126a), in the passage "Bless the Lord, O my soul" (Psalms 104:1), which we quoted in the Gate of Awe, chapter 12: at the end of that passage, when David considered the judgments a person [faces] when he departs from this world, he anticipated and said, "Bless the Lord, O my soul," before you leave the world — now that you have joined with the body, and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:32: Further, there is also proof in the Zohar (Parashat Vayikra 12b) that rising at midnight benefits the purification of thoughts. It says there that the psalm, "Behold, bless the Lord, all you servants of the Lord" (Psalms 134:1), is said regarding those who stand to occupy themselves with Torah at midnight; and it says, who are those whose praise is entirely for the King? It continues and says, "who stand in the house of the Lord by night" — these are called "servants of the Lord"; these are worthy to bless the King, and their blessing is a [true] blessing — this is what is written, "lift up your hands to the sanctuary and bless the Lord" (Psalms 134:2) — you are worthy that the holy King be blessed through your hands, and the blessing that comes through your hands is a [true] blessing — so far his words. Since it says that the supernal King is blessed through him, certainly his thoughts are correct and pure; and when he is confused and not in [proper] thought, his blessing is not a blessing and his unification is not a unification — rather, certainly, Heaven will assist him to become fully righteous and for his thought to be holy. This is among the virtues of rising at midnight to occupy oneself with Torah, for it is explained in Parashat Vayikra that the Torah makes known to him his sin so that he may repent; so it is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Vayikra 23b), on the verse, "or his sin, which he has committed, be made known to him" (Leviticus 4:23), in these words: whoever rises at night to occupy himself with Torah — the Torah makes known to him his sin, not in the manner of strict judgment, but like a mother who makes known to her son with soft words, and he does not forget it, and returns in repentance before his Master. And should you say, David used to rise at midnight, why then was judgment aroused against him? Rather, David was different, for he transgressed in that to which he was bound and required judgment, and by what he transgressed he was judged — he sinned against the holy kingship, and so on — so far his words, as pertains to us.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:33: There is further proof for this matter from the passage we quoted in Parashat Vayikra (13a), which says further on that concerning the aforementioned "servants of the Lord" it is said, "lift up your hands to the sanctuary and bless the Lord," and explains there that this is the mystery of the supernal Chochmah, which is Eden, called "the sanctuary" (kodesh). Certainly, if there is no attachment in his soul to the place of holiness, he cannot draw a blessing from there to the Lord; rather, certainly he first becomes sanctified from there, and through this he can afterward draw a blessing from there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:34: And so it is explained in the Zohar (there, Parashat Lech Lecha 92b) that one who rises to occupy himself with Torah nurses from the "stream of the ancients" (nachal kedumim), in these words: Rabbi Chizkiah said, whoever occupies himself [with Torah] at that hour certainly has a constant portion in the World to Come. Rabbi Yosei said, why "constant"? He said to him, this is what I have learned: at every midnight, when the Holy One, blessed be He, stirs in the Garden of Eden, all the plantings of the garden are watered further from that stream called "the stream of the ancients," "the stream of delights," whose waters never cease; as it were, that one who stands and occupies himself with Torah is as though that stream were poured over his head and waters him among those plantings in the Garden of Eden. Rabbi Yosei said, since all the righteous within the Garden of Eden listen to him, they give him a portion in that watering of the stream; it follows that he has a constant portion in the World to Come — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:35: When you examine what is explained in the Tikkunim (88a) regarding "the stream of the ancients, the stream of delights," it will not seem far-fetched that his thought becomes sanctified, for he nurses from the holy place, since that stream is poured over his head, and therefore he can draw a blessing from there; and it is fitting that the thought resting in his head should be sanctified.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:36: However, in order to merit being holy with the holiness of thought as explained, his Torah study must be a clean Torah — for if he is wicked, his Torah is repugnant, as it is written, "but to the wicked God says, what have you to do with declaring My statutes?" (Psalms 50:16); and one cannot say of him that the righteous give him a portion in that watering of the stream, for he is pushed away from there through his own deeds.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:37: Further, regarding what the passage says, that he is called a "servant of the Lord" — "Behold, bless the Lord, all you servants of the Lord, who stand in the house of the Lord by night" — the intent of "standing in the house of the Lord by night" is that his image stands and is engraved above in the Shechinah, who is "the house of the Lord," and she says, "See with what I have been aroused toward you" (Zohar Parashat Vayikra 13a). One cannot say that "standing in the house of the Lord" means literally that a person is studying in a synagogue, which is specifically "the house of the Lord" — for we find several stories in the Zohar, of Rashbi's colleagues, peace be upon him, who studied at night in their own homes, particularly when they were exiled from their homes and studied in caves and villages — specifically in the Zohar (Parashat Lech Lecha 92b), in the story of the village of Tarsha, where their study in the house of lodging was at midnight. Rather, certainly the correct interpretation is as we have explained — that one "stands in the house of the Lord," having merited through his deeds that his image be engraved above, in the house of the Lord. But if he is wicked, his image is erased from the house of the Lord, and even if he occupies himself with Torah, his Torah does not effect an arousal. Therefore, whoever wishes to merit this quality must be a complete penitent, and then Heaven will assist him so that his image be engraved above, to be called a "servant of the Lord," and to draw from the holiness, and the other virtues explained and to be explained, please God.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:38: Among the conditions of a penitent is that he rise at night to confess and weep over his sins, as is elaborated in Chovot HaLevavot, peace be upon him. And so King David, peace be upon him, said, "I anticipated the twilight and cried out..." (Psalms 119:147), and said, "I remember Your Name, O Lord, in the night, and keep Your Torah" (Psalms 119:55) — the intent being that because he remembers His Name, blessed be He, at night with songs and praises, this is the cause that "I keep Your Torah," as explained above, that one who rises at midnight subdues the Other Side.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:39: This is what it says right after, "This has become mine, that I have kept Your precepts" (Psalms 119:56). According to the plain sense, it means: this aforementioned quality, that I remembered His Name, blessed be He, at night, is what has caused me to keep Your precepts. And according to the mystical sense, because one who rises at night joins with "this" (zot), which is the Shechinah, and since he joins with her, the Shechinah does not allow him to be pushed away from her or let the evil inclination rule over him to cause him to sin — since he wishes to be among the servants of the Lord, they assist one who comes to purify himself — this is [the meaning of] "that I have kept Your precepts," in the manner stated. And so it likewise says, "O Lord, God of my salvation, by day I cry out, at night before You" (Psalms 88:2), and "my salvation" — its essential meaning is to save me from the hand of the evil inclination, as is explained in the Zohar. If so, it is fitting for every penitent who rises at night to occupy himself with Torah, that he first confess and weep over his sins, and afterward Heaven will assist him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:40: Now, besides the aspect of the holiness of thought that depends on rising at midnight, as we have explained, there is in rising at midnight a general holy aspect for a Torah scholar, which pertains to the discourse of this Gate we are engaged in; and this aspect is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Kedoshim 81a), in these words: Rabbi Abba said, why are the portion of forbidden relations and the portion of "you shall be holy" adjacent to one another? Rather, we have learned thus: whoever guards himself from these forbidden relations is certainly made holy, and all the more so if he sanctifies himself with the holiness of his Master. Now the colleagues have discussed when is the time appropriate for a person to sanctify himself. Come and see, whoever wishes to sanctify himself with the will of his Master should not have marital relations except from midnight onward, or at midnight itself — for at that hour the Holy One, blessed be He, is found in the Garden of Eden, and supernal holiness is aroused, and then is the time to sanctify oneself. This applies to other people; but Torah scholars, who know the ways of Torah, their time is midnight, to rise and occupy themselves with Torah, to join with the Community of Israel, to praise the holy Name, the holy King. But on Sabbath night, when the will of all is found, their union is at that hour, to bring forth the will of the Holy One, blessed be He, and the Community of Israel, as it is said, as it is written, "You are children to the Lord your God" (Deuteronomy 14:1); and these are called holy, as it is written, "You shall be holy, for I the Lord am holy" (Leviticus 19:2), and it is written, "and he shall be like a tree planted by streams of water, that brings forth its fruit in its season" (Psalms 1:3) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:41: This passage makes clear that the time of union for the rest of the people on weekdays, which is at midnight, is the time for Torah scholars to sanctify themselves in the union of the Community of Israel, rising to occupy themselves with Torah; it follows that they sanctify themselves in a spiritual and holy union, in place of what the rest of the people sanctify themselves in a physical union. But on Sabbath night, when the Community of Israel unites above and does not need arousal from the Torah of the souls of the righteous — this being the meaning of "when the will of all is found" — that is, the will above is found of itself and does not need us — then their union at that hour is to bring forth the will of the Holy One, blessed be He, and the Community of Israel, and so on. This is because the union on Sabbath night is in Atzilut, which is not the case on the six weekdays, when the union is below, in Metatron.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:42: And so it is explained in the Tikkunim (93), in these words: and on Shabbat, which is the seventh day, there is the closeness and unification of the Name YHVH and likewise the [other] sefirot; therefore Torah scholars have their union from Sabbath night to Sabbath night. These forbidden relations [restrictions] certainly apply below; but above it is said, "evil shall not sojourn with You" (Psalms 5:5), and a righteous man who has relations with his wife on the weekdays — that son whom he begets is regarded such that it is said of him, "a righteous man, and it is evil for him" (Ecclesiastes 8:14), for he causes the holy to become mundane, since it is the seventh day [in a spiritual sense for him]; and at that time it is the mystery of "a righteous man, and it is evil for him" — so far his words. And what it says regarding a righteous man who has relations with his wife, and so on, we must say applies to a righteous man who has a soul of Atzilut, which is holy, and therefore he causes the holy to become mundane; but if he has a soul of Metatron, which is mundane, it is mundane joined to mundane, and it is not a blemish — and this is the union of the rest of the people, which is at midnight on the six weekdays, as explained above, because their soul is from there.
